items.text: So Baan Noi runs about 22 dollars a head. Which is fair I guess for what you get and its a good pad see ew they have good texture, the noodles actually taste like something. Green curry is loaded with sugar and its cloying. That is not the only thing that dragged our meal down. We got there on a Friday and the wait was long. Kitchen is clearly in over its head. So if you go there you'll get a decent meal but you'll have to put up with slow service. But you can get the same result at a bunch of other places around town, the good stuff is just as easy to get at the bad. I'd rather eat somewhere that gets both right.

We stayed at Encore and it was an easy walk over to the show. O was on hiatus so we tried La Rêve instead. La Rêve gets compared to O, possibly even derivative of it, I assumed it was fine. The show may or may not have a story that I didn't understand but it didn't matter to me. There's a pre-show act of a comic lizard swimming in the pool, holding still, and then he suddenly lunges forward to startle people sitting in front. The main spectacle is the pool and its platforms that rise and lower, with performers swimming, diving, and even walking on water. There's a huge 25 foot or so dive off the main stage. If you're looking for a good major vegas show but don't want to pay Cirque du Soleil money, this was well worth it. We left impressed but it wasn't O.

Myself and the family went to see La Rêve. We were going to see O but its on hiatus. So we book La Rêve. I know La Rêve is often compared to O, maybe even based on O and I figured if O is not possible, La Rêve is pretty good alternative. We were at Encore so walking distance to the show. We had seat about row 3. Now La Rêve might have a story, but I didn't follow it, but that was fine with me. Before the main performance a comedy guy who looks like a lizard swims in the pool. Stays still for a long time, looks like statue and then sneaks up to front row and sprays water. Its really good show, main performance with platform rising and lowering, people swimming and diving and walking on water. Dive from 25 feet above the pool. If you want to see a big show in Vegas, not so expensive as Cirque du Soleil, I recommend La Rêve. Very impressed.

We meant to see O, but it was on hiatus so we did La Rêve. The hotel was Encore and it was an easy walk. We got 3rd row seats. I knew people compare La Rêve to O so it seemed like a fair substitute. It isn't O of course. But it's a good substitute.
I don't think La Rêve has a story or maybe it does, I did not understand it, whatever. Pre-show there is some funny guy in a lizard suit swimming in the pool and he just sits there like a statue for a really long time. Then he will quietly swim to the front rows and blast them with water.
The main show is very impressive. Pool with platforms going up and down and then all this swimming and diving, walking on water stuff, and they do a dive from about 25 feet above the pool. Anyway, I think if you really want a show in Vegas that is not expensive like Cirque du Soleil, get La Rêve, go for it. We came out very impressed.

So a rain gauge works pretty simply: you catch rain in a circular hole that's a specific size. A funnel feeds it into a measuring tube that's marked off at regular intervals for the depth like millimeters or inches. It reads how deep the rain is assuming it fell in a flat plain and no runoff or soaking in of it. Usually the opening is wider than the measuring tube, so that makes it easier to read it, the scale on the measuring tube is adjusted for the size of the hole. Now the problem is placement, so if you put your gauge near a tree or building or a fence you might get too little or too much because of sheltering or splashing. Also evaporation can be a problem too. If you don't read it soon after the storm, you lose water.

rain gauges are really simple actually. they measure rain by catching it through a circular opening of known area, and the water gets funneled into a tube, marked in mm or inches. it just tells you how deep it would have been if it rained evenly over the ground and none soaked in. the opening tends to be wider than the little tube on the side, which concentrates all the water into a narrower column and gets to make the small amounts of rain read easier. the scale is adjusted for that difference in area so the reading is still the depth. two main ways this is inaccurate, I think. placement is a big one. trees, buildings, fences close to it, or something like that and it'll be too little or too much because of sheltering or splashing in. And then just not reading it soon enough and evaporation is happening.

This rain gauge works in a dead simple way. You put rain in and the rain falls through the round top, and you know the area. And the water then falls down into a tube which is like measuring tube, and it has a scale on it. And you read it off in depth units, millimetres, inches etc, and that's how deep it would have been on the ground. It's like if you don't have any run-off or soak in etc, how deep it would be. But often the top bit is wider than the tube, so it concentrates it into a thinner tube, so if it's a low rain it's easier to read it. And it's adjusted, the scale's adjusted to compensate for the different areas. And the two things that tend to screw up the gauge are the position, placing it near trees or buildings or fences, etc, it'll either get sheltered and it won't rain into it or it'll splash in etc. And also evaporation, that's another problem. So you should try and read it immediately after the rain, otherwise you'll get evaporation and it'll make it read lower.

Marguerite finds this book every Thursday. Same spot, between flour bins and the cooling racks, like it just climbs in through the wall. Spine is cracked, a faded library stamp, due date long passed. Eleven Thursdays. She asked the day staff, checked locks, even stayed late once with her thermos and a rolling pin but never caught the moment. It appears between two and four in the morning, just there. Tonight it's heavier. When she opened it, a folded square of receipt paper slid out. She read it twice. I keep meaning to return it to the library but walk past your window on the way and the light is on, think somebody's awake, leave it there instead. Sorry. I'll stop if you ask me to. Behind her the ovens ticked, first trays of rye waiting under cloths. She flipped the receipt over. A pencil stub was behind her ear. Wrote on the back. Don't stop. Tucked it back inside the cover. Set the book on the sill next to the front window, left the light on.

240 am. The sour tang of fermenting rye is always there, overpowers the floor bleach no matter how much you mop. Arthur wiped his palms on his jeans, went behind the wicker bannetons. There, on the bottom wire rack, lay the library’s taped-up copy of The Count of Monte Cristo. It was the fourth Thursday, and like the others, its spine sat flush with the steel edge.

He pulled it out. Stuck on the cover was a square piece of blue prescription notepad in ballpoint ink, written on so hard the letters go through the paper. It said: “The baker in chapter five reminds me of you. Thank you for keeping the lights on.” Arthur traced the deep indents from the pen with his thumb. Only sound was the compressor shuddering. A slip of paper fell off the back of the book. Yellowing, a due-date card stamped faded red, three days overdue.

He went to the prep table, wrapped up a warm, glaze-mapped cinnamon roll in parchment paper and put it in his coat pocket with the book.

Arthur walked to the prep table and wrapped a warm cinnamon roll in parchment, glaze mapped on the surface, and put it in his coat pocket next to the book.

I'm keeping it, four stars. Space bar rattles, hit it with thumb edge and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key repeats too, so eexample, I backspace to fix. Happens maybe once an afternoon and only when I'm typing fast, not looking. I paid $38 but still keeping because the switches. Asked seller what they were and answer took a week. Book drop was a milk crate by the back door. Every Thursday around two, Imre would find something in there that wasnt milk. First week he got A Field Guide to Mushrooms of the Northeast, Carver Street Library stamp on the flyleaf, due date long past. Second week the same. Third week the same. He stopped reshelving it in his head. It lived on the flour bench now, between the scale and the tub of rye starter, cover gone soft with dough-dusted thumbprints.

Tonight he slid the crate out with his hip, hands still in oven mitts. The book was there again, heavier than usual. A yellow square of paper stuck out near page 112. Peeled off the mitts. The note was in pencil, small, slanted hard to the right. It said, Your door smells better than the library. I keep meaning to bring it to the right place. Is the morel on this page the one you use? Signed T. Imre looked at the page. No one had circled anything, the morel just sat there, wrinkled and brown. Pulled the pencil from behind his ear, flipped the note over and wrote, No. Never used one. Then after a moment he added, Come at five, there's bread. Pressed it back into the book.

At 3:17 in the morning Marisol heard the walk in cooler kick on and the proofing cabinet breathe. She slid the first loaves into the oven. In the wicker basket by the back door the worn paperback, The Borrowers, sat again. Its checkout card was blank in the back just a barcode and a coffee ring on it. Someone had left the book at her bakery instead of the library two blocks over for six Thursdays.
She wiped her hands on her apron. There was a folded note tucked between pages 84 and 85.
I can’t get to the library before it closes. Please keep it here another week. I like knowing it’s warm.
She looked at the basket, then the tray of cinnamon rolls cooling on the rack. She picked the one with the most icing and wrapped it in wax paper. Tucked the note back into the book and set both by the door. At 4:50 she pulled the loaves out and knocked them from their pans then slid the next tray in the oven.

I paid 38 dollars for this used keyboard, second hand. Modest hopes, no missing caps, no mystery grime on the switches, didn't feel like gravel. On that scale it did fine. Clean enough to go on my desk no major cleaning. I like the weight of the keys, very good for long emails. I type a lot. After long sessions my fingers don't get beat up as much as they do with some newer cheap keyboards. Rough edges there. The space bar rattles when I hit it off center, little clack and makes the board sound cheaper than it feels. One key repeats every once and a while. I keep finding extra letters in middle of sentences. Not all the time but annoying. Communication was a weak spot with the seller. I asked what switches it was. It took them a week to answer by the time it came. So i just took the key cap off and looked. I thought about returning it but I saw myself packing it up and paying to ship it back. For 38 I kept it. It's flawed but usable.

It showed up clean enough that I just put it on my desk and started using it without having to do a full clean project. And the keys have a nice weight to them. I type a ton of long emails and this board is really good for that. My fingers don't feel wrecked after a long stretch which I can't say for some of the newer cheap boards.

Rough edges aren't hidden on it. The spacebar does this rattling sound every time I hit it off centre. Its kind of a loose little clack that makes it sound cheaper then it feels. And one key does this repeating every now and then. You'll be typing and look up and there's this extra letter in the middle of a sentence. Not all the time, but annoying.

There's also a key that repeats now and then so I can be typing, look up, see an extra letter in the middle of a sentence. Not a constant issue but it gets annoying. Communication was a problem. I asked the seller what switches are on it. They answered the question a week later. By the time I got the response I had already ripped the keycap off to see what was in there. I considered returning it. But then when I pictured the effort of packing it and paying the postage to ship it back I figured, for $38 it's good enough. It's imperfect but usable.

I've been to Vegas my whole life, well the under 21 version. Sat through lots of shows before I could gamble. Le Reve at Wynn is one I finally got to see. Honestly its mixed. Slightly worse than mixed. The round stage works well. You look down into it. So any seat you'll get a good view. That's rare in Vegas. Some acts were cool. The strength things, aerialist stuff, divers. Those guys are athletes. But it just feels like Cirque du Soleil. Not necessarily a ripoff but if you've seen Cirque you've seen things like that so it's not groundbreaking, just done a bit more clearly. The issue is clarity. What's the story? Still don't know. Dreams? A man? Water? Felt like images thrown at you and nothing telling us what it was saying. And it was way too much going on. Too many people, too many things, too many wow moments one after the other. Something more reserved would have worked better. Feels like that stereotypical Vegas show thing, more must be better. So they crammed too much in. Tickets are 125 but Wynn and Encore residents get 99. So that's helpful. But would I see it again? Probably not. Pay for it a second time? No. It was just okay, aside from a few stunts. Not blown away. Don't think anyone else was either. Some friends did enjoy it. So if you haven't seen it and you want to, why not go once. Just don't expect to be blown away.

Too many people too many elements too many wow moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. Ticket note. If you're staying at wynn or encore, they have a deal. $99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would i see it again? Probably not, and i wouldn't pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts it was just average. I wasn't blown away and i don't think anyone else was either. That said a few friends liked it and if you've never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don't expect to leave overwhelmed.

It was 3:40 in the morning. The second batch of rye was still proofing. Marisol found the book again, sitting on the flour bin by the back door, its plastic jacket cold from the alley. Fourth Thursday in a row now. Same book, A Field Guide to Night Birds, Eastgate Branch, and every single week a new due-date slip. She'd put it in the return box on the way home each time, and by the next Thursday somebody would have checked it out and brought it back here. She scraped dough off her knuckles and opened it. On the barn owl page where somebody had penciled a checkmark next to 'call: a long, harsh scream', a folded card had fallen out. It read: You leave the vent fan on. The alley reeks of bread until five. I walk my mother's dog at half past three because she can't anymore. Heard one of these behind the dumpster. Keep checking this out again. — R. Marisol read the card twice. The oven timer was counting down. Outside, the fan was rattling steam across the wet dumpster lid. She turned the card over and with the grease pencil she uses to mark trays, wrote: Rye's out at 4:15. Then she wrapped a heel from yesterday's loaf in wax paper, put it on the outside step, laid the book on top of that, and propped the back door open just about an inch.
